tier_reason: BENCHMARK.md gives first-party KITTI 00 results against pcl::VoxelGrid (1.3x single-thread, 3.2x with 6 TBB threads) and pcl::GICP / fast_gicp::GICP (2.4x / 1.9x), with public scripts (scripts/run_downsampling_benchmark.sh, run_odometry_benchmark.sh, src/benchmark/). No CPU model (only a struck-through AMD 5995WX remark), compiler or flags are stated for these runs, beyond CMake defaulting to Release and -march=native being off by default, so it is C. The JOSS 2024 paper (source docs/paper.md) only repeats the same first-party bullets, and JOSS reviews software, not benchmarks, so it does not lift the tier to B.

corrections.caveats: Baselines are PCL and fast_gicp, not Boost.Geometry, CGAL or GEOS, so it fits the geometry-spatial category only loosely (point-cloud spatial operations). Its kd-tree is nanoflann-derived and README says the single-thread build is about equal to nanoflann. The multi-thread kd-tree gain is stated three ways: BENCHMARK.md 'up to 4x' over its own single-thread build, README 'up to 6x' over the single-thread version, and the JOSS paper source (docs/paper.md) 'up to 6x faster than that of nanoflann'. Benchmark scripts are public, but CPU, compiler and flags are not stated for the PCL comparisons, and only KITTI 00 was used. The JOSS paper repeats the README bullets and adds no independent measurement.

notes: All quoted ratios appear verbatim in BENCHMARK.md and in the README Benchmark section. The vcpkg port named in stars_or_usage was not checked (the repo page does not mention it). joss.theoj.org is egress-blocked, so the paper was read from its source file in the repo.

tier_reason: The README Criterion output compares rand_xoshiro::Xoshiro256Plus (33.10 ns per 64 u64) with the portable and AVX-512 Xoshiro256+X8 (7.51 / 7.08 ns) on a stated Ryzen 9 9950X3D. The code is public (benches/top/mod.rs, run by 'make bench-top'), and the flags are stated (.cargo/config.toml target-cpu=native, Makefile AVX-512 RUSTFLAGS, release profile opt-level 3, LTO, codegen-units 1). But the toolchain is an unpinned 'cargo +nightly' with no rustc version, which earlier waves held to C (e.g. Criterion benches with no rustc version).

corrections.claimed_speedup: Scalar rand_xoshiro Xoshiro256+ 33.10 ns per batch of 64 u64 (1.93 Gelem/s) versus portable Xoshiro256+X8 7.51 ns (8.52 Gelem/s) and AVX-512 Xoshiro256+X8 7.08 ns (9.04 Gelem/s): about 4.4x and 4.7x (derived from page data). For the author's frand generator, the scalar upstream frand crate (autovectorised by the compiler) runs 3.18 ns and FrandX8 2.53 ns, only about 1.26x (derived from page data). The 13x figure in the earlier record compared FrandX8 with scalar Xoshiro256+, which is a different generator. README text: vectorised PRNGs 'may perform anywhere from 4-6 times faster'.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: cargo +nightly (rustc version not stated; MSRV 1.89). .cargo/config.toml sets -C target-cpu=native; bench-top adds RUSTFLAGS -C target-feature=+avx2,+avx512f,+avx512dq,+avx512vl; release profile opt-level 3, lto = true, codegen-units = 1; pinned to one SMT pair with taskset and the performance governor
corrections.caveats: The speedup compares the same algorithm scalar versus lane-parallel, so it measures vectorisation, not a better algorithm. Checked: the portable and AVX-512 Xoshiro256+X8 lanes run the standard xoshiro256+ step (s0+s3 output, s1<<17, rotl 45), and FrandX8 lanes match the upstream frand crate (the crate's tests assert this), so the SIMD paths compute the named generators as 8 independent streams. FrandX8::seed_from_u64 copies one seed into all 8 lanes, so the lanes emit identical streams. Seed with distinct from_seed bytes for independent lanes; the timed FrandX8 rows used seed_from_u64. Benchmarks accumulate batches into u64x8 to keep the work observable, which favours wide registers. frand is the author's choice of a small generator, and the README says he is no expert in statistical testing (PractRand only). The latest commit is 'fix frand implementation (#34)'. README warns that older AVX-512 CPUs may throttle.

notes: All README numbers match the record. The tier drops only because the rustc nightly version is unstated; everything else needed for A is present. The RNG same-generator check passed for Xoshiro256+X8 against rand_xoshiro::Xoshiro256Plus.

tier_reason: The README prints the full BenchmarkTools code and output for Base randn!/rand! against local_rng(). The AVX-512 run is followed by versioninfo(): Julia 1.6.0-DEV.1581, LLVM 11.0.0 ORCJIT tigerlake (default JIT optimisation) on an Intel Core i7-1165G7. That meets A, as with Octavian.jl in this wave. The Haswell AVX2 numbers lack a CPU model and are C-level on their own.

corrections.caveats: Numbers are from 2020 on a Julia 1.6 dev build. The README says Base Julia used dSFMT only up to 1.7, so the baseline no longer describes current Julia (Base now uses its own Xoshiro256++). The README itself says dSFMT 'in a few tests appears to outperform this library on AVX2 systems' for uniform numbers, and that the normal-distribution win comes mainly from a SIMD Box-Muller versus a scalar ziggurat. The AVX2 machine's CPU model is not given. Correctness: despite the 'vectorized Xoshiro256++' label, src/xoshiro.jl outputs rotate_right(s0+s3, 23) without the '+ s0' term (left commented out), and it updates s3 with rotate_right(s3, 45), which equals a left rotation by 19, not xoshiro's left rotation by 45. VectorizationBase defines rotate_right as a true right funnel shift. So the engine is a nonstandard xoshiro-like variant, and the standard xoshiro256 jump constants it uses to space streams 2^128 apart are not valid for that engine; full period and stream separation are not established. It passes SmallCrush in CI and BigCrush per the README. Baseline is not std::mt19937.

notes: All eight timings match the README. The same-generator rule does not void the claim, because the baseline is a different generator (Base MersenneTwister) by design. The mislabelled generator is still a shortcoming worth recording.
